tier_reason: The arXiv paper, published in peer-reviewed form in IEEE TDSC 2025 (DOI 10.1109/TDSC.2025.3575915), compares against the pq-crystals AVX2 code and states gcc-9.4.0, the flags and the i7-11700F CPU, so the floor is B. It is not A because the paper never links the anonymous GitHub repo ('We will later open source our code'; empty README). The repo also holds only Round3 Dilithium, not the FIPS 204 ML-DSA code behind the headline numbers, and its Makefile flags differ from the paper's.

corrections.baseline: pq-crystals/dilithium AVX2 optimized implementation (Round3 NIST submission, and FIPS 204 ML-DSA from the pq-crystals 'standard' branch); liboqs was not benchmarked
corrections.claimed_speedup: Abstract figures 43.2%/39.3%/45.6% (KeyGen), 36.6%/41.6%/43.7% (Sign), 45.3%/46.5%/47.4% (Verify) are cycle-count reductions vs AVX2, not +% speedups. They come from Table XI (FIPS 204 ML-DSA-44/65/87), even though the abstract labels them Dilithium2/3/5. As ratios (derived from page data): KeyGen 1.76x/1.65x/1.84x, Sign 1.58x/1.72x/1.78x, Verify 1.83x/1.87x/1.90x. For Round3 Dilithium2/3/5 (Table IX, the code in the repo), cycle reductions vs AVX2 are KeyGen 55.5%/65.1%/58.6%, Sign 50.0%/52.8%/56.6%, Verify 55.0%/56.2%/58.5% (derived ratios 2.25x/2.87x/2.42x, 2.00x/2.12x/2.31x, 2.22x/2.28x/2.41x). NTT 13.95x and INTT 17.94x are vs 1-way scalar code (Table VIII), not vs AVX2.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Paper: gcc-9.4.0, -Wshadow -Wpointer-arith -mavx2 -mavx512f -mavx512vbmi -mavx512bw -mavx512cd -mavx512vl -mpopcnt -maes -march=native -mtune=native -O3. The repo Makefile instead uses cc with -mavx512f -mavx512bw -mavx512cd -mavx512vl -mavx512dq -mavx2 -mpopcnt -maes -march=native -mtune=native -O3 (dq, no vbmi).
corrections.caveats: No LICENSE file, so redistribution terms are unclear. The repo is from an anonymous org, has an empty README and is not linked from the paper, so its provenance as the paper's artifact is unconfirmed. It contains only Round3 Dilithium AVX-512 code; the FIPS 204 ML-DSA code behind the abstract numbers is not public. The paper's percentages are cycle reductions, and the paper says constant-time was not the focus. Needs an AVX-512 CPU. No commits since 2023-07-18. The benchmarks are the authors' own and have not been independently reproduced.

notes: The paper is now peer-reviewed (IEEE TDSC 2025), so B is solid. If the TDSC version turns out to link this repo, the Round3 Table IX numbers could reach A. The record's '+43.2%' framing overstated the gain: 43.2% fewer cycles is about 1.76x.

tier_reason: The paper is peer-reviewed (IEEE TPDS 2024, DOI 10.1109/TPDS.2024.3367319) and its Table 6 compares GPU throughput against the Falcon AVX2 CPU implementation, so B. It is not A because the paper gives no compiler, flags, thread count or even which CPU ran the AVX2 baseline (Table 4 lists only 'CUDA 11'). The repo has no AVX2 baseline harness, and its released code covers only Falcon-512 and Mitaka-512.

corrections.baseline: Falcon NIST-submission AVX2-optimized CPU implementation (Fouque et al. [4]); Mitaka is compared only against its FP64 reference C. liboqs was not benchmarked.
corrections.claimed_speedup: The paper's stated ratios do not match its own tables. '7.78x sign / 52.43x verify vs AVX2' (RTX 3080, Falcon-512) is actually vs the FP64 reference (27908/3587, 1913380/36491). 'Falcon-1024 20.56x/148.56x' equals A100 Falcon-512 throughput divided by AVX2 Falcon-1024 throughput. The abstract's '20.03x/29.51x' equals Mitaka-512 on A100 vs the Mitaka FP64 reference. Recomputed from Tables 5/6, Falcon GPU batch throughput (K=16384) vs AVX2 CPU (derived from page data): Falcon-512 RTX 3080 8.81x sign / 104.96x verify; Falcon-1024 RTX 3080 5.35x / 66.45x; Falcon-512 A100 18.50x / 149.29x; Falcon-1024 A100 13.18x / 114.24x.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GPU: CUDA 11 (paper Table 4); repo Makefile uses CUDA 11.7 nvcc -rdc=true -arch sm_86 with gcc as the host compiler. Compiler/flags for the CPU AVX2 baseline are not stated anywhere in the paper.
corrections.hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3080 (8704 CUDA cores; desktop host Intel i9-10900K @3.70GHz) plus A100/V100/T4 on the ARDC Nectar cloud (host Intel Xeon Gold 6150 @2.2GHz). The paper does not say which CPU or how many threads produced the AVX2/FP64 CPU baseline rates in Table 6.
corrections.workload: Falcon-512/1024 batched signing and verification throughput on GPU (K up to 16,384 signatures per launch) vs the Falcon AVX2-optimized CPU implementation; Mitaka-512/1024 GPU vs the Mitaka FP64 reference C
corrections.caveats: This compares a GPU batch against a CPU implementation of unstated thread count, so the >50x verify ratios are a hardware and batching effect. Per-batch latency is high (e.g. 587 ms for a 16,384-signature Falcon-512 sign batch on the RTX 3080). The paper's own speedup text misattributes baselines (see claimed_speedup). Released code covers only Falcon-512 and Mitaka-512, targets sm_86, and has no CPU baseline harness. It rebuilds the LDL tree on every signature. No commits since 2023-11-14.

notes: The main fix is claimed_speedup: none of the record's three headline ratio pairs is actually Falcon-vs-AVX2 per the paper's own Tables 5/6, so I replaced them with ratios recomputed from the page data. Metadata (GPL-3.0, 5 stars, last commit 2023-11-14, stale, copyable) checks out.

tier_reason: Upgraded C to A. The paper's anonymous artifact is reachable through the anonymous.4open.science API (README, Apache-2.0 LICENSE, and the benchmark Makefiles all fetched). It ships generator/benchmark/kyber/ref and dilithium/ref (unmodified pq-crystals baselines) next to kyber_plan_plannorm/ref and dilithium_plan/ref, with 'make speed' test_speed harnesses at -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer. The paper states gcc-11.4, the flags and the Intel Xeon E-2314 CPU.

corrections.baseline: NIST PQC / pq-crystals reference C implementations of ML-KEM (Kyber ref) and ML-DSA (Dilithium ref) for end-to-end and NTT results, plus formosa-mlkem Jasmin (NTT only); mlkem-native/mldsa-native scalar C (OPT=0 AUTO=0) is compared only at NTT level
corrections.claimed_speedup: End-to-end vs pq-crystals reference C (Table 3): ML-KEM-512 decaps 1.32x, encaps 1.27x, keygen 1.17x (ML-KEM-768/1024 1.13-1.24x); ML-DSA-2 sign 1.26x, verify 1.16x, keygen 1.11x (ML-DSA-3/5 1.08-1.25x). NTT vs reference C: forward 1.47-1.83x, inverse 1.66-2.48x (Table 1). Vs formosa-mlkem Jasmin, ML-KEM NTT 1.26x and INTT 2.19x (round-trip 1.63x); these are kernel-level numbers, not end-to-end. Vs mlkem-native scalar C, the ML-KEM forward NTT is slower (0.86x) and INTT is 1.18x; vs mldsa-native, 1.66x/1.52x (Table 2).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc-11.4 -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer (C, matching the pq-crystals test_speed setup); Jasmin 2025.6.1 + clang-14 -O3 -march=native -fomit-frame-pointer -fwrapv (verified backend); 10k iterations, rdtsc with cpuid, median of three per-run medians
corrections.caveats: This is a 2026 ePrint preprint and not yet peer-reviewed. The code lives only at a double-blind-review anonymous.4open.science mirror (https://anonymous.4open.science/r/pkc_anonymous_artifact-8F22). Its web UI redirects, but its API serves the files. Links like this are temporary. All wins are over scalar reference C: no AVX2 backend is provided (the authors measured Plantard ~28% slower than Montgomery under AVX2), so this does not beat the optimized AVX2 ML-KEM/ML-DSA implementations, and the forward ML-KEM NTT loses to mlkem-native scalar C (0.86x). The Apache-2.0 license is from an anonymous copyright holder.

notes: The artifact the search agent could not open (HTTP 401) is reachable via https://anonymous.4open.science/api/repo/pkc_anonymous_artifact-8F22/file/<path>. repo_url could be set to the anonymous artifact URL, though it is ephemeral. The record's baseline was wrong: end-to-end gains are vs pq-crystals reference C, not mlkem-native/mldsa-native or liboqs.
